lessons.title: Content words vs function words
lessons.explain: English is stress-timed: you stress the words that carry meaning and squeeze the rest.
points: Strong: nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs, question words.

items.text: I want to go to the store.
items.pattern: I WANT to GO to the STORE.

items.text: She is looking for a new job.
items.pattern: she's LOOKing for a NEW JOB.

items.text: Can you give me a hand?
items.pattern: can you GIVE me a HAND?

items.text: We have been waiting for an hour.
items.pattern: we've been WAITing for an HOUR.

lessons.title: Emphasis changes the meaning
lessons.explain: Move the strongest word and the message changes completely. Say each line and hear the new meaning.
points: Stress the word you want to correct or highlight.

items.text: I never said she stole it.
items.pattern: I NEVER said she stole it.

items.text: I never said she stole it.
items.pattern: I never SAID she stole it.

items.text: I never said she stole it.
items.pattern: I never said SHE stole it.

items.text: I never said she stole it.
items.pattern: I never said she stole IT.

lessons.title: Question words carry the stress
lessons.explain: In WH- questions, the question word itself is usually strong.

items.text: What time is it?
items.pattern: WHAT time is it?

items.text: Where do you live?
items.pattern: WHERE do you LIVE?

items.text: Why did you do that?
items.pattern: WHY did you DO that?

items.text: Who told you that?
items.pattern: WHO told you THAT?

lessons.title: Contrastive stress
lessons.explain: When comparing two things, stress the word that shows the difference.

items.text: I ordered coffee, not tea.
items.pattern: I ordered COFfee, not TEA.

items.text: She's my sister, not my friend.
items.pattern: she's my SIStr, not my FRIEND.

items.text: We're leaving today, not tomorrow.
items.pattern: we're leaving toDAY, not toMORrow.

items.text: He's the manager, not the owner.
items.pattern: he's the MANager, not the OWner.

lessons.title: New information gets the stress
lessons.explain: In a conversation, the newest piece of information is usually the strongest word — already-known information gets weaker.

items.text: A: Where's John? B: John is in the KITCHen.
items.pattern: 'John' is already known, so 'kitchen' is stressed.

items.text: A: What did you buy? B: I bought a NEW LAPtop.
items.pattern: 'bought' is known from the question, so the object is stressed.

items.text: A: Who called? B: My BROTHer called.
items.pattern: new info = brother.

lessons.title: Stress in negative sentences
lessons.explain: The negative word (not / never / n't) is often stressed to make the denial clear.

items.text: I don't like it.
items.pattern: I DON'T like it.

items.text: She isn't coming tonight.
items.pattern: she ISn't coming tonight.

items.text: We can't afford it.
items.pattern: we CAN'T afford it.

items.text: That's not what I meant.
items.pattern: that's NOT what I meant.

lessons.title: Stress in polite requests
lessons.explain: Even polite, softly-spoken requests keep clear stress on the content words.

items.text: Could you help me, please?
items.pattern: could you HELP me, please?

items.text: Would you mind closing the window?
items.pattern: would you mind CLOsing the WINdow?

items.text: Do you have a minute?
items.pattern: do you have a MINute?

lessons.title: Stress on modal verbs for meaning
lessons.explain: Modals like can, should and must are usually weak — but stressing them changes the meaning to add certainty or surprise.

items.text: You should call her.
items.pattern: you should CALL her.

items.text: You SHOULD call her.
items.pattern: you SHOULD call her.

items.text: He CAN speak French!
items.pattern: he CAN speak French!

lessons.title: Everyday small talk sentences
lessons.explain: Practise stress on common small-talk lines you'll say every day.

items.text: How's it going?
items.pattern: HOW's it GOing?

items.text: Long time no see!
items.pattern: LONG time no SEE!

items.text: Nice to meet you.
items.pattern: NICE to MEET you.

items.text: Have a good weekend.
items.pattern: have a GOOD WEEKend.

lessons.title: Stress in comparisons
lessons.explain: In comparative sentences, both the adjective and the comparison word usually get stress.

items.text: This one is bigger than that one.
items.pattern: this one is BIGger than THAT one.

items.text: She's much taller than her brother.
items.pattern: she's MUCH TALLer than her BROther.

items.text: It's the best restaurant in town.
items.pattern: it's the BEST resTAUrant in TOWN.

lessons.title: Stress in giving opinions
lessons.explain: Opinion phrases carry stress on the key opinion word, not on 'I think' itself.

items.text: I think it's a great idea.
items.pattern: I think it's a GREAT idea.

items.text: In my opinion, it's too expensive.
items.pattern: in my oPINion, it's too exPENsive.

items.text: Personally, I'd rather stay home.
items.pattern: PERsonally, I'd RAther stay HOME.

lessons.title: Stress in phone conversations
lessons.explain: Phone-call English has its own set of common stressed phrases.

items.text: Can I speak to Sarah, please?
items.pattern: can I SPEAK to SARah, please?

items.text: She's not available right now.
items.pattern: she's not aVAILable right NOW.

items.text: Can I take a message?
items.pattern: can I TAKE a MESsage?

lessons.title: Stress when giving directions
lessons.explain: Direction-giving relies on clear stress so the listener catches the key landmarks and turns.

items.text: Turn left at the traffic light.
items.pattern: TURN LEFT at the TRAFfic light.

items.text: It's right next to the bank.
items.pattern: it's RIGHT NEXT to the BANK.

items.text: Go straight for two blocks.
items.pattern: go STRAIGHT for TWO BLOCKS.

lessons.title: Stress in requests for clarification
lessons.explain: When you didn't understand, stress the question word or the part you missed.

items.text: Sorry, what did you say?
items.pattern: SORry, WHAT did you SAY?

items.text: Could you repeat that, please?
items.pattern: could you rePEAT that, please?

items.text: What do you mean by that?
items.pattern: WHAT do you MEAN by that?

lessons.title: Stress with 'too' and 'either'
lessons.explain: 'Too' and 'either' at the end of a sentence usually take their own beat of stress.

items.text: I love this song too.
items.pattern: I LOVE this SONG TOO.

items.text: I don't like it either.
items.pattern: I DON'T like it EIther.

items.text: She's coming too.
items.pattern: she's COming TOO.

lessons.title: Stress in job-interview answers
lessons.explain: Interview English needs confident, clear stress on your strongest selling points.

items.text: I'm a fast learner and a team player.
items.pattern: I'm a FAST LEARner and a TEAM PLAYer.

items.text: My biggest strength is problem-solving.
items.pattern: my BIGgest STRENGTH is PROBlem-SOLving.

items.text: I'm excited about this opportunity.
items.pattern: I'm exCIted aBOUT this opporTUNity.

lessons.title: Stress when correcting a mistake
lessons.explain: When correcting yourself or someone else, the corrected word gets extra stress.

items.text: No, I said Tuesday, not Thursday.
items.pattern: no, I said TUESday, not THURSday.

items.text: It's spelled with an 'e', not an 'a'.
items.pattern: it's spelled with an 'E', not an 'A'.

items.text: Actually, it's twenty dollars, not twelve.
items.pattern: actually, it's TWENty dollars, not TWELVE.

lessons.title: Stress in shopping conversations
lessons.explain: Shopping English — practise clear stress so you're understood at the till or in a fitting room.

items.text: Do you have this in a smaller size?
items.pattern: do you have this in a SMALLer SIZE?

items.text: How much does it cost?
items.pattern: HOW MUCH does it COST?

items.text: Can I try it on?
items.pattern: can I TRY it ON?

lessons.title: Stress with reflexive emphasis (myself, himself)
lessons.explain: Reflexive pronouns used for emphasis ('I did it myself') always get a strong stress.

items.text: I did it myself.
items.pattern: I did it my-SELF.

items.text: She fixed the car herself.
items.pattern: she fixed the car her-SELF.

items.text: They built the house themselves.
items.pattern: they built the house them-SELVES.

lessons.title: Stress in giving instructions
lessons.explain: Clear, imperative instructions rely on stress to sound confident and easy to follow.

items.text: Press the button and wait.
items.pattern: PRESS the BUTton and WAIT.

items.text: Don't forget to save your work.
items.pattern: DON'T forGET to SAVE your WORK.

items.text: Make sure it's plugged in.
items.pattern: make SURE it's PLUGGED in.

lessons.title: Stress in apologies
lessons.explain: Apology phrases still need the right stress to sound sincere, not flat.

items.text: I'm really sorry about that.
items.pattern: I'm REAlly SORry about THAT.

items.text: It won't happen again.
items.pattern: it WON'T HAPpen aGAIN.

items.text: I should have told you sooner.
items.pattern: I SHOULD have TOLD you SOOner.

lessons.title: Stress on numbers in context
lessons.explain: When giving prices, dates or quantities, the number itself is almost always the strongest word.

items.text: It costs fifty dollars.
items.pattern: it costs FIFty DOllars.

items.text: The meeting is at three o'clock.
items.pattern: the MEEting is at THREE o'clock.

items.text: We need six more copies.
items.pattern: we need SIX more COpies.

lessons.title: Stress in storytelling
lessons.explain: Good storytelling exaggerates the stress on the most dramatic or surprising words.

items.text: And then, suddenly, the lights went out!
items.pattern: and then, SUDdenly, the LIGHTS went OUT!

items.text: I couldn't believe what I was seeing.
items.pattern: I COULDn't beLIEVE what I was SEEing.

items.text: It was the best day of my life.
items.pattern: it was the BEST day of my LIFE.

lessons.title: Stress with 'even' for emphasis
lessons.explain: 'Even' adds surprise, and the word right after it usually carries the strongest stress.

items.text: Even my dad likes this song.
items.pattern: even my DAD likes this song.

items.text: I didn't even notice.
items.pattern: I didn't even NOtice.

items.text: She finished even faster than me.
items.pattern: she finished even FASTer than me.

lessons.title: Stress in conditional sentences
lessons.explain: In 'if' sentences, stress the condition and the result — the connecting words stay weak.

items.text: If it rains, we'll stay home.
items.pattern: if it RAINS, we'll STAY HOME.

items.text: If I were you, I'd apologize.
items.pattern: if I were YOU, I'd aPOLogize.

items.text: I would have come if you'd asked.
items.pattern: I WOULD have COME if you'd ASKED.

lessons.title: Stress in reported speech
lessons.explain: Reporting verbs (said, told, asked) are usually weak — the actual message carries the stress.

items.text: She said she'd be late.
items.pattern: she said she'd be LATE.

items.text: He told me not to worry.
items.pattern: he told me not to WORry.

items.text: They asked if we were coming.
items.pattern: they asked if we were COMing.

lessons.title: Stress when making suggestions
lessons.explain: Suggestion phrases stress the activity being suggested, not the suggestion frame itself.

items.text: Why don't we get some coffee?
items.pattern: why don't we get some COFfee?

items.text: How about going for a walk?
items.pattern: how about going for a WALK?

items.text: Let's try that new restaurant.
items.pattern: let's try that NEW resTAUrant.

lessons.title: Stress in talking about future plans
lessons.explain: Plans and intentions stress the activity and the time reference.

items.text: I'm meeting a friend tomorrow.
items.pattern: I'm MEETing a FRIEND toMORrow.

items.text: We're planning to move next year.
items.pattern: we're PLANning to MOVE next YEAR.

items.text: I might travel this summer.
items.pattern: I might TRAVel this SUMmer.

lessons.title: Stress in talking about past experiences
lessons.explain: Past experience talk stresses the event and any time markers, common in IELTS Speaking Part 2.

items.text: I visited Japan two years ago.
items.pattern: I VISited JaPAN two YEARS ago.

items.text: I've never tried sushi before.
items.pattern: I've NEver TRIED SUshi beFORE.

items.text: That was the best trip I've ever had.
items.pattern: that was the BEST TRIP I've Ever had.

lessons.title: Stress when expressing likes and dislikes
lessons.explain: The verb of feeling and the thing you like or dislike both usually get stress.

items.text: I really love this song.
items.pattern: I REALly LOVE this SONG.

items.text: I can't stand waiting in line.
items.pattern: I CAN'T STAND WAITing in LINE.

items.text: I'm not really a fan of spicy food.
items.pattern: I'm not REALly a FAN of SPIcy FOOD.

lessons.title: Stress describing a process step by step
lessons.explain: Sequence words (first, then, after that, finally) get their own beat when explaining a process.

items.text: First, you boil the water.
items.pattern: FIRST, you BOIL the WAter.

items.text: Then you add the pasta.
items.pattern: THEN you ADD the PASta.

items.text: Finally, drain it and serve.
items.pattern: FInally, DRAIN it and SERVE.

lessons.title: Stress comparing pros and cons
lessons.explain: Balanced pro/con sentences stress the contrasting sides clearly, common in IELTS Part 3 discussion answers.

items.text: On the one hand it's cheaper, but on the other hand it takes longer.
items.pattern: CHEAPer ... LONGer

items.text: The main advantage is speed, while the main drawback is cost.
items.pattern: SPEED ... COST

lessons.title: Stress agreeing and disagreeing
lessons.explain: Agreement and disagreement phrases stress the key word that shows your position.

items.text: I completely agree with you.
items.pattern: I comPLETEly aGREE with you.

items.text: I see your point, but I disagree.
items.pattern: I SEE your POINT, but I disaGREE.

items.text: That's exactly what I think too.
items.pattern: that's exACTly what I THINK too.

lessons.title: Stress in restaurant ordering
lessons.explain: Ordering food stresses the dish name and any specific requests.

items.text: I'll have the grilled chicken, please.
items.pattern: I'll have the GRILLED CHICKen, please.

items.text: Could I get that without onions?
items.pattern: could I get that withOUT ONions?

items.text: Can we get the check, please?
items.pattern: can we get the CHECK, please?

lessons.title: Stress apologizing for being late
lessons.explain: A sincere apology stresses the reason and the apology word itself.

items.text: Sorry I'm late, the traffic was terrible.
items.pattern: SORry I'm LATE, the TRAFfic was TERrible.

items.text: I'm so sorry for the delay.
items.pattern: I'm SO SORry for the deLAY.

lessons.title: Stress describing someone's appearance
lessons.explain: Descriptions of people stress the distinguishing feature you're highlighting.

items.text: She's the one with the curly hair.
items.pattern: she's the ONE with the CURly HAIR.

items.text: He's tall and always wears glasses.
items.pattern: he's TALL and ALways wears GLASSes.

lessons.title: Stress in emergency and urgent phrases
lessons.explain: Urgent phrases exaggerate stress on the key danger word so the listener reacts fast.

items.text: Call an ambulance now!
items.pattern: CALL an AMbulance NOW!

items.text: Watch out, the floor is wet!
items.pattern: WATCH OUT, the FLOOR is WET!

items.text: We need help immediately.
items.pattern: we NEED HELP imMEdiately.

lessons.title: Stress talking about deadlines and time pressure
lessons.explain: Workplace time-pressure phrases stress the deadline and the consequence.

items.text: The report is due by Friday.
items.pattern: the rePORT is DUE by FRIday.

items.text: We're really pressed for time.
items.pattern: we're REALly PRESSED for TIME.

items.text: Can we push the meeting back an hour?
items.pattern: can we PUSH the MEETing BACK an HOUR?

lessons.title: Stress in casual invitations
lessons.explain: Casual invites stress the activity and the time, keeping the invitation frame itself weak.

items.text: Do you want to grab lunch later?
items.pattern: do you want to GRAB LUNCH LAter?

items.text: We're having a party this weekend.
items.pattern: we're HAVing a PARty this WEEKend.

items.text: You should totally come with us.
items.pattern: you should TOtally COME with us.

lessons.title: Stress talking about abilities and skills
lessons.explain: Talking about what you can and can't do stresses the skill itself, not the modal verb.

items.text: I can speak three languages.
items.pattern: I can SPEAK THREE LANGuages.

items.text: I'm not very good at cooking.
items.pattern: I'm not VEry GOOD at COOKing.

items.text: She's really talented at drawing.
items.pattern: she's REALly TALented at DRAWing.

lessons.title: Stress expressing surprise
lessons.explain: Surprised reactions stress the unexpected part of the news heavily, often with extra pitch too.

items.text: I can't believe you did that!
items.pattern: I CAN'T beLIEVE you DID that!

items.text: No way, that's amazing!
items.pattern: no WAY, that's aMAZing!

items.text: Seriously? I had no idea.
items.pattern: SEriously? I had NO iDEa.

lessons.title: Stress making a complaint
lessons.explain: Complaints stress the problem word clearly, so the listener understands exactly what's wrong.

items.text: This isn't what I ordered.
items.pattern: this ISN'T what I orDERED.

items.text: I've been waiting for over an hour.
items.pattern: I've been WAITing for Over an HOUR.

items.text: This is the second time this has happened.
items.pattern: this is the SECond TIME this has HAPPened.

lessons.title: Stress describing your daily routine
lessons.explain: Routine descriptions stress the action verbs and time markers, common in IELTS Part 1.

items.text: I usually wake up at seven.
items.pattern: I usually WAKE UP at SEVen.

items.text: I always check my email first.
items.pattern: I ALways CHECK my EMail FIRST.

items.text: I try to exercise every morning.
items.pattern: I TRY to EXercise EVery MORNing.

lessons.title: Stress talking about the weather forecast
lessons.explain: Weather talk stresses the condition and the time it's expected.

items.text: It's supposed to rain tomorrow.
items.pattern: it's supposed to RAIN toMORrow.

items.text: It's going to be really hot this week.
items.pattern: it's gonna be REALly HOT this WEEK.

lessons.title: Stress discussing a news story
lessons.explain: Talking about news stresses the key facts — who, what and the outcome.

items.text: Did you hear about the new policy?
items.pattern: did you HEAR about the NEW POLicy?

items.text: Apparently the price is going up next month.
items.pattern: apPARently the PRICE is going UP next MONTH.

lessons.title: Stress giving a warning
lessons.explain: Warnings stress the danger and the action needed, spoken with extra force.

items.text: Be careful, the road is icy.
items.pattern: be CAREful, the ROAD is ICy.

items.text: Watch your step, it's slippery here.
items.pattern: WATCH your STEP, it's SLIPPery HERE.

lessons.title: Stress offering choices at a shop or counter
lessons.explain: Offering options stresses each choice being offered.

items.text: Would you like paper or plastic?
items.pattern: would you like PAper or PLAStic?

items.text: Do you want that for here or to go?
items.pattern: do you want that for HERE or to GO?

lessons.title: Stress with wishes and hypotheticals
lessons.explain: Wishes and hypothetical statements stress the imagined situation strongly.

items.text: I wish I had more free time.
items.pattern: I WISH I had MORE FREE time.

items.text: If only I'd studied harder.
items.pattern: if ONly I'd STUDied HARDer.

lessons.title: Stress talking about birthdays and celebrations
lessons.explain: Celebration talk stresses the event and the special detail about it.

items.text: We're throwing a surprise party for her.
items.pattern: we're THROWing a surPRISE PARty for her.

items.text: It's my brother's birthday next week.
items.pattern: it's my BROTHer's BIRTHday next WEEK.

lessons.title: Final mixed review
lessons.explain: A closing mixed set pulling together content words, emphasis and negatives — mark the stress before checking.

items.text: I really need this done by Friday.
items.pattern: I REALly NEED this DONE by FRIday.

items.text: I didn't say it was easy.
items.pattern: I DIDn't SAY it was EAsy.

items.text: She's the one who called, not him.
items.pattern: she's the ONE who CALLED, not HIM.
